mcqs.question: Why is inorder traversal the natural choice for reading a binary search tree's values in sorted order?
options: Because inorder always visits the root first
Because inorder is the only traversal that runs in O(n) time
Because inorder is required for tree serialization
Because visiting left subtree, then node, then right subtree exactly matches the BST invariant that everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger
mcqs.explanation: The BST invariant guarantees every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger, and inorder's left-node-right visiting order walks through exactly that structure, producing ascending order as a direct consequence. Inorder doesn't visit the root first (that's preorder), all three traversal orders are O(n), and serialization more commonly uses preorder with null markers.

mcqs.question: Why is iterative postorder traversal harder to implement with a single stack than preorder or inorder?
options: Postorder requires two separate stacks by definition
A plain stack pop can't tell whether a node's right subtree has already been fully processed, since postorder needs both children done before visiting the node itself
Postorder cannot be implemented iteratively at all
Postorder visits nodes in a different total order than recursion produces
mcqs.explanation: The core difficulty is that visiting a node requires confirming its right subtree is finished, which a stack's contents alone don't reveal — the standard fix tracks a 'last visited' node to resolve that ambiguity explicitly. Postorder is fully achievable iteratively (just harder), a two-stack variant exists as an alternative but isn't required, and it produces the identical visiting order as the recursive version.

mcqs.question: Recursive and iterative (explicit-stack) tree traversal have the same O(h) space complexity in principle. Why might the recursive version still fail on a tree the iterative version handles fine?
options: The recursive version has strictly worse time complexity
A language's call stack often has a much lower configured depth limit than its heap memory, so a very deep tree can overflow the call stack while heap-backed iteration keeps working
Recursive traversal cannot visit all nodes correctly
Iterative traversal uses O(1) space, unlike recursion's O(h)
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches carry the same O(h) space bound, but a language's call stack is typically capped far below available heap memory, so a sufficiently skewed, deep tree can hit that recursion limit even though an equivalent iterative structure using heap-allocated storage would not. Time complexity is identical between the two, correctness is unaffected by the choice, and iterative traversal still uses O(h) space, not O(1).

mcqs.question: What does Morris traversal do to achieve O(1) extra space, instead of using a stack or recursion?
options: It processes only half the tree's nodes
It converts the tree into an array first
It requires the tree to already be a valid BST
It temporarily threads a null right pointer of the inorder predecessor to point back at the current node, using that thread instead of a stack to know when to return
mcqs.explanation: By temporarily repurposing an otherwise-unused null right pointer as a 'come back here' link, Morris traversal eliminates the need for any auxiliary stack or recursion, visiting every node while using only a constant number of extra variables. It visits every node, doesn't require array conversion, and works on any binary tree, not just BSTs.

mcqs.question: A Morris traversal implementation creates threads correctly but never removes them afterward. What's the consequence?
options: The traversal output itself becomes incorrect
The traversal crashes with an infinite loop
The traversal's output is still correct, but the tree is left with extra incorrect right pointers, corrupting its structure for any later operation on it
Nothing — thread removal is an optional optimization with no functional effect
mcqs.explanation: The output sequence itself doesn't depend on removing the threads, so the function can appear to work perfectly — but the tree's actual pointer structure is left altered, with fake right-child links that don't represent real edges, which silently breaks anything that touches the tree afterward. This isn't optional cleanup and it doesn't cause an infinite loop within the traversal itself; the damage surfaces later, elsewhere.
